body.heading: Why worries visit at night
paragraphs: The mind often saves its worrying for bedtime for an unflattering reason: it is the first quiet moment of the day. All the concerns that were outrun by activity line up in the dark, each one convinced it will be forgotten by morning unless it keeps you awake guarding it.

That last part is the lever. Much of the looping is not problem-solving; it is your mind acting as a reminder system that does not trust you to remember. Give it a better system, and it can stand down.

body.heading: The five-minute download
paragraphs: An hour or so before bed — not in bed — take a notebook and write, in scruffy shorthand, everything circling: tasks, worries, half-decisions, things to buy, people to call. Beside each, add the smallest next step or the time you will think about it tomorrow. “Email Sam, 9 a.m.” is a complete entry.

Then close the notebook, literally. The closing is part of the signal: these are parked, in writing, where morning-you will find them. Nothing needs to be solved tonight because nothing can be lost tonight.

body.heading: If thoughts return anyway
paragraphs: Some nights they will come back regardless. When they do, you can answer them with the truth: “It is written down. It has a time.” Then return your attention to something dull and kind — your breathing, the weight of the blanket, counting backwards slowly from three hundred.

If racing thoughts at night are a long-standing pattern that is damaging your days, mention it to a doctor. There is specific, effective help for persistent insomnia, and it starts with exactly that conversation.

takeaway: Write it down, close the book, and let the paper do the remembering tonight.
